paragraphs: As long as several men assembled together regard themselves as a single body, they have only one will, which is concerned with their common preservation and general well-being. In that case all the workings of the State are vigorous and simple, and its rules are clear and bright. There are no tangles or conflicts of interest; the common good shows itself plainly everywhere, and only good sense is needed to see it. Peace, unity and equality are the enemies of political subtlety. Upright, simple men are hard to deceive precisely because they are simple: tricks and clever pretexts do not work on them, and they are not even subtle enough to be dupes. When we see bands of peasants, among the happiest people in the world, settling the affairs of State under an oak tree and always acting wisely, can we help despising the refined methods of other nations, which make themselves famous and miserable with so much art and mystery?

A State governed this way needs very few laws. When it becomes necessary to issue new ones, everyone sees the necessity. The first man to propose them merely says what all have already felt. There is no need for factions, intrigues or eloquence to get a law passed that everyone has already resolved to follow, as soon as he is sure the others will do likewise.

Theorists go wrong because they see only States that were badly constituted from the start, and they are struck by how impossible it would be to apply such a policy to them. They have great fun imagining all the absurdities that a clever rascal or a smooth talker could get the people of Paris or London to believe. They do not know that the people of Berne would have put Cromwell to “the bells,” and the Genevese would have put the Duc de Beaufort on the treadmill.

But when the social bond starts to loosen and the State to weaken, when particular interests begin to be felt and smaller societies begin to influence the larger one, the common interest changes and meets opposition. Opinion is no longer unanimous. The general will stops being the will of all. Contradictory views and debates arise, and even the best advice is accepted only after being challenged.

Finally, the State stands on the eve of ruin and keeps up only a vain, illusory, formal existence. The social bond is broken in every heart, and the meanest interest brazenly seizes the sacred name of “public good.” Then the general will falls silent. All men, guided by secret motives, no longer give their views as citizens, any more than if the State had never existed, and unjust decrees aimed solely at private interest are passed under the name of laws.

Does it follow that the general will is destroyed or corrupted? Not at all. It is always constant, unalterable and pure, but it is overridden by other wills that encroach on its territory. Each man, in separating his interest from the common interest, sees clearly that he cannot separate them entirely. But his share in the public misfortunes seems trivial next to the exclusive good he hopes to make his own. Setting aside this particular good, he wills the general good in his own interest as strongly as anyone else. Even when he sells his vote for money, he does not extinguish the general will in himself; he only evades it. His fault is to change the question, and to answer something other than what he is asked. Instead of saying with his vote, “It is to the advantage of the State,” he says, “It is to the advantage of this man or that party that this or that view should win.” So the law of public order in assemblies is less to maintain the general will there than to make sure that the question is always put to it, and that the answer is always given by it.

Here I could set down many reflections on the simple right to vote in every act of Sovereignty — a right no one can take from the citizens — and also on the right to state opinions, make proposals, divide and discuss, which the government is always most careful to leave to its own members alone. But this important subject would need a treatise of its own, and it is impossible to say everything in a single work.
